bio.en: Dalton Caldwell is a managing director and group partner at Y Combinator, where he's worked with more startups than nearly anyone alive, and previously co-founded and led imeem and App.net.
bio.zh: Dalton Caldwell 是 Y Combinator 的管理董事兼集团合伙人，他合作过的初创公司数量几乎无人能及，此前曾联合创立并领导 imeem 和 App.net。

summary.en: Dalton distills startup wisdom from seeing thousands of applications: sell something, make money, and above all “don't die.” He covers what to do when your startup is struggling, how to know when to pivot (a good pivot feels like going home), and why avoiding over-delegation early matters. The conversation also lists startup ideas to avoid and 20 categories of ideas he's actively looking to fund.
summary.zh: Dalton 从审阅数千份申请中提炼出创业智慧：卖东西、赚钱，最重要的是“别死”。他讲述了创业陷入困境时该做什么、何时该转型（好的转型像回家一样），以及早期为何避免过度授权。对话还列出了该避开的创业点子，以及他正积极寻找投资的 20 类点子。

turns.en: So to prep for this podcast interview, I asked a bunch of founders that worked with you during YC what advice you shared with them along the journey that was most transformative to the way they think about product, the way they think about building their startup, the way they operate. Why do you think founders need to hear this advice, which is seemingly simple and obvious?
turns.zh: 因此，为了准备这次播客采访，我询问了在 YC 期间与您共事的一群创始人，您在整个旅程中与他们分享了哪些建议，这些建议对他们对产品的思考方式、他们对建立初创公司的思考方式以及他们的运营方式最具变革性。出现了很多主题，我将讨论其中的一些主题。这些主题之一就是你多久会得到非常简单的实用建议，以及你的信息有多少只是卖狗屎，赚钱，不要把钱花光。您认为为什么创始人需要听到这个看似简单明了的建议？

turns.speaker: Dalton Caldwell
turns.en: Have you ever seen in NBA basketball or college basketball where they have the coach mic'd up and it shows what they're actually saying in the huddle? You're at the top of your game if you make it to the elite levels of being a startup founder or basically doing anything that's really hard psychologically. (00:06:33): And so yeah, one of my mantras is just don't die. Just keep your startup going. Just keep going. And I say that over and over again and honestly, that is often what people tell me is the most impactful thing I said. It's not that I said some Ninja 5D chess mood that they never would've thought of before. It's just the constant affirmation that continuing to keep going and doing high quality reps is the game.
turns.zh: 您是否曾在 NBA 篮球或大学篮球比赛中见过教练将麦克风打开并显示他们在人群中实际所说的话？你有听过他们实​​际上在说什么吗？他们会说，“好吧，我们需要真正集中注意力，拿到球并赢得这场比赛。”如果你真的听听最伟大、最聪明、最成功的运动员在谈论什么，如果你听听泰格·伍兹对他的球童说的话，这一切听起来都是很平常的事情。老虎伍兹与他的球童谈论的并不是一些难以理解的行话。就像是，“是的，你真的需要在这件事上保持低调。”就是这样的事情。我认为这是正确的原因是，即使你处于世界上最好的水平，接受指导并提醒你基本原理和基础知识会让你处于正确的心态，并且你已经知道一切，对吗？如果你达到了创业公司创始人的精英水平，或者基本上做了任何心理上非常困难的事情，那么你就处于游戏的顶端。 (00:06:33)：是的，我的口头禅之一就是不要死。只要让你的创业公司继续下去。继续吧。老实说，我一遍又一遍地这么说，人们常常告诉我，这是我说过的最有影响力的事情。并不是我说了一些他们以前想不到的忍者5D棋意。这只是不断地肯定，继续前进并做高质量的代表就是游戏。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I know that you'd give a talk that's exactly called that, How Not To Die. Just to pull on this thread a little bit more, what is the general advice you share there for people that also don't want to die?
turns.zh: 我知道你会做一个演讲，名字就叫“如何不死”。只是为了进一步拉动这个话题，您对那些也不想死的人分享的一般建议是什么？

turns.speaker: Dalton Caldwell
turns.en: The way to summarize that is if you look at all the startup stories that we have at YC and all the companies we funded over all the years, the underlying theme is that rationally the founder should have given up at some point. And so again, let's talk about Airbnb, obviously something you know a lot about. They probably should have shut down three or four times before they got into YC. It objectively wasn't working. They were basically ruining their lives, they were disappointing their parents, everything was wrong and it was a purely irrational act for the founders of Airbnb to keep working on their goofy startup. And again, that's just one story. If you look across the portfolio of YC and non-YC companies, there has to be this irrational intention to keep going even when the world tells you it's not working and you feel completely defeated. And you likely have to go through this many times and have these near-death experiences. And then you get lucky and then you look like an overnight success. Right? (00:08:26): And so that is the theme that is a summary and I provide lots of data and lots of stories there, but this is one of those things that the longer I have this job, the more I really, really believe this is true.
turns.zh: 总结一下，如果你看看我们在 YC 的所有创业故事以及我们多年来资助的所有公司，潜在的主题是，从理性上讲，创始人应该在某个时候放弃。再次，我们来谈谈 Airbnb，显然您对此非常了解。他们在进入 YC 之前可能应该关闭三四次。客观上它没有发挥作用。他们基本上毁了自己的生活，让父母失望，一切都错了，Airbnb 的创始人继续致力于他们愚蠢的初创公司纯粹是非理性的行为。再说一次，这只是一个故事。如果你纵观 YC 和非 YC 公司的投资组合，你就会发现，即使世界告诉你这不起作用并且你感到彻底失败，你仍然会继续前进，这是一种非理性的意图。你可能必须经历很多次，并有这些濒临死亡的经历。然后你就很幸运，看起来就像一夜暴富。正确的？ (00:08:26)：这就是总结的主题，我在那里提供了大量的数据和故事，但这是我从事这份工作的时间越长，我就越真的、真的相信这是真的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What's your advice on the flip side of that where there's a lot of startups, especially these days that are just super struggling, have been added for a while, there are mental health challenges, they'd be very sad if they had to shut this thing down, but often it's probably the right move? What's your advice to folks on deciding, okay, actually does make sense to give up in this case?
turns.zh: 另一方面，你有什么建议，因为有很多初创公司，特别是现在，它们的处境非常艰难，已经添加了一段时间，存在心理健康挑战，如果他们不得不关闭这个东西，他们会非常难过，但通常这可能是正确的举动？对于在这种情况下决定放弃实际上是否有意义的人们，您有什么建议？

turns.speaker: Dalton Caldwell
turns.en: I think this is a nuanced question and it's hard for me to say something on a podcast that'll actually be useful to people, but here's a couple of thoughts. One, are you still having fun? Do you still enjoy doing what you're doing? Do you enjoy spending time with your co-founders? Is this actually a fun thing you're doing? And if the answer there is yes, I would tend to lean on the keep going. And then if it's more of, wow, this is actually profoundly affecting me a negative way and my relationships with people in my life and I don't really want to work with my co-founder anymore and things like that, then I would lean on the probably don't do it anymore. Something that a lot of the folks that turn it around have in common is they actually do love their customers and they love their product. (00:09:51): And again, in the Airbnb story, again, you know it really well, but they really liked Airbnb and they liked working with each other and they liked the first host that they met and they knew all their names. You know what I'm saying? They loved their startup even though it was going bad. And so that's to me a signal to keep going is that you really, really love what you're doing and the people you're doing it with and you love your customers and you love the problem. Versus where you're just like, "Yeah, I could care less about any of those things. I'm just having a bad time." Harder to be encouraging in that situation. And this is a fixable situation. You can make it more like the thing you love, can't you?
turns.zh: 我认为这是一个微妙的问题，我很难在播客上说一些对人们实际上有用的东西，但这里有一些想法。一、你还玩得开心吗？你仍然喜欢做你正在做的事情吗？您喜欢与联合创始人共度时光吗？这实际上是你正在做的一件有趣的事情吗？如果答案是肯定的，我会倾向于继续前进。然后，如果更多的是，哇，这实际上对我以及我生活中与人的关系产生了深远的负面影响，而且我真的不想再与我的联合创始人一起工作以及类似的事情，那么我可能会不再这样做。许多扭转局面的人都有一个共同点，那就是他们确实爱他们的客户，也爱他们的产品。 (00:09:51)：再说一次，在 Airbnb 的故事中，你非常清楚这一点，但他们真的很喜欢 Airbnb，他们喜欢互相合作，他们喜欢他们遇到的第一位房东，而且他们知道他们所有人的名字。你知道我在说什么吗？他们热爱自己的创业公司，尽管它的情况很糟糕。所以这对我来说是一个继续前进的信号，那就是你真的、真的热爱你正在做的事情以及和你一起做事的人，你热爱你的客户，你热爱这个问题。而你会说，“是的，我可以不在乎这些事情。我只是过得很糟糕。”在这种情况下更难鼓励。这是一个可以解决的情况。你可以让它更像你喜欢的东西，不是吗？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. This is actually very practical and great advice. This is something people can sense, "Okay, am I actually enjoying this? Do I want to keep doing this?" Versus, "Man, such a drag that I have to keep running this startup." Is there anything you could say to folks that are just like, "I can't stop because it'll feel like I failed"?
turns.zh: 是的。这实际上是非常实用且很好的建议。这是人们可以感觉到的，“好吧，我真的喜欢这个吗？我想继续这样做吗？”与“伙计，这真是太累了，我必须继续经营这家​​初创公司。”你有什么话可以对那些“我无法停下来，因为我会觉得自己失败了”的人说吗？

turns.speaker: Dalton Caldwell
turns.en: If it's really going poorly or if you're having a really bad time, it's no big deal. No one will remember that you shut down your company probably in 10 years or 20 years time. As long as you have integrity, as long as you're an honest person, as long as you handle yourself well through good times and bad, people will remember you fondly. We have such a short life. There's only so many years we get to have our careers, doing something that makes you miserable and the only reason you're doing it is to avoid losing face and you know in your heart is not going to work, I don't know, that seems like a pretty big opportunity cost on literally your life. Right?
turns.zh: 如果事情真的很糟糕或者你过得很糟糕，那也没什么大不了的。没有人会记得你可能会在 10 年或 20 年后关闭你的公司。只要你有正直，只要你是一个诚实的人，只要你在顺境和逆境中处理好自己，人们就会深深地记住你。我们的一生如此短暂。我们的事业只有这么多年，做一些让你痛苦的事情，你这样做的唯一原因是为了避免丢脸，你心里知道这是行不通的，我不知道，这似乎对你的生活来说是一个相当大的机会成本。正确的？

turns.en: Yeah, that's exactly what I tell founders all the time. Life is short. There's no need to force yourself to work on this. And I really like your point of just, is it still enjoyable? Do you like working with your founders? Following this thread of the struggle training a little bit more, one of the founders that worked with you during YC, his name is Danny Alberson, shared a story how during one of the batches of YC, one of the founders raised his hand and asked you, "What is wrong with our batch? Everyone is struggling, nobody is doing well. What have we done wrong?" And you shared a story about Brex that made everyone feel a little better. Does that ring a bell and if so, can you share that?
turns.zh: 是的，这正是我一直告诉创始人的。生命是短暂的。没有必要强迫自己去做这件事。我真的很喜欢你的观点，它仍然令人愉快吗？你喜欢和你的创始人一起工作吗？沿着这条斗争训练的线索再多一点，在 YC 期间与你一起工作的一位创始人，他的名字叫 Danny Alberson，分享了一个故事，在 YC 的其中一批中，一位创始人举手问你，“我们这批出了什么问题？每个人都在挣扎，没有人做得很好。我们做错了什么？”你分享了一个关于 Brex 的故事，这让每个人都感觉好一点了。这是否引起了人们的注意？如果是的话，您能分享一下吗？

turns.speaker: Dalton Caldwell
turns.en: That definitely happened and I think the story is the story of the Winter-17 batch. And in the Winter-17 batch, I funded something like, I don't know, 35, 40 companies in my group. So we subset them into groups. So it wasn't a lot of companies and I knew all of them really well. And founders can't help but compare themselves with other founders all the time about who's doing well and who's not doing well. And there was this one company in my group, this batch, it was called Vyond, that was their name at the time and it was a VR headset thing from these Stanford dropouts. And they basically showed up to group office hours and were just ashamed and they're like, "Our idea is horrible. We might want to shut our company down. This is really embarrassing." I had to beg them to not give up basically. And if you would've asked people in the batch what the worst company was, I think they would've said this one. Again, not because they were bad people but the founders themselves seemed despondent about how it was going. (00:13:13): And then funnily enough, this is in the story too, there was another startup also in my group called Cashew, which was this P2P Venmo, excuse me, in the UK and it was going really poorly also and not growing. And so if you just took this snapshot in time in the middle of the batch of who is definitely not doing well, it would clearly have been this Vyond company and this Cashew company. And so to cut to the chase, Vyond changed their idea and got really excited about it and renamed to Brex and this was Brex, which is like a decacorn. And Cashew changed their idea and renamed to something called Retool. And so out of my 35 companies, the ones that objectively seemed the worst in terms of everything is going bad, were by far, in retrospect, the most successful companies in that group.
turns.zh: 这确实发生了，我认为这个故事就是第 17 届 Winter 批次的故事。在 17 年冬季批次中，我资助了我团队中的 35 家、40 家公司，我不知道。所以我们将它们分组。所以公司并不多，而且我对他们都很了解。创始人总是情不自禁地与其他创始人进行比较，看看谁做得好，谁做得不好。我的团队里有一家公司，这一批，它叫 Vyond，这是他们当时的名字，这是斯坦福大学辍学学生推出的一款 VR 耳机。他们基本上出现在集体办公时间，只是感到羞愧，他们会说，“我们的想法太糟糕了。我们可能想关闭我们的公司。这真的很尴尬。”我不得不恳求他们基本上不要放弃。如果你问这批人中最糟糕的公司是什么，我想他们会说这家。再说一遍，并不是因为他们是坏人，而是创始人本身似乎对事情的进展感到沮丧。 (00:13:13)：有趣的是，这也在故事中，我的团队中还有另一家名为 Cashew 的初创公司，这是 P2P Venmo，对不起，在英国，它的发展也非常糟糕，而且没有增长。所以，如果你在这批表现肯定不好的人中间及时拍下这张快照，那显然就是这家 Vyond 公司和这家 Cashew 公司。因此，为了切入正题，Vyond 改变了他们的想法，并对此感到非常兴奋，并将其重命名为 Brex，这就是 Brex，就像一个十角兽。 Cashew 改变了他们的想法，并更名为 Retool。因此，在我的 35 家公司中，那些客观上看起来一切都在恶化的最糟糕的公司，回想起来，却是该组中最成功的公司。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow. Wait, so you're saying Brex was a VR headset company?
turns.zh: 哇。等等，你是说 Brex 是一家 VR 耳机公司？

turns.speaker: Dalton Caldwell
turns.en: They thought it was really high-tech. They want to do a really high-tech startup, and so they're like, "We're going to build a new VR headset." And yeah, they were good programmers, but they just didn't know anything about optics or the things you might want to be an expert in to build a headset.
turns.zh: 他们认为这确实是高科技。他们想做一家真正高科技的初创公司，所以他们会说，“我们要打造一款新的 VR 耳机。”是的，他们是优秀的程序员，但他们只是对光学或你可能想成为构建耳机的专家的东西一无所知。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow, that's an amazing story. It's a great segue to just another theme that emerged from talking to founders about advice that you've shared. A lot of people tell me you are the king of the pivot of helping people figure out how to pivot. I'm curious just what you've seen makes a good pivot.
turns.zh: 哇，这是一个了不起的故事。这是对另一个主题的一个很好的延续，这个主题是在与创始人讨论你分享的建议时出现的。很多人告诉我，你是帮助人们弄清楚如何进行转型的转型之王。我很好奇你所看到的是什么构成了一个很好的支点。

turns.speaker: Dalton Caldwell
turns.en: Usually a successful pivot gets warmer instead of colder from what you're an expert at and somehow builds on what you learned on the prior idea. Right? And so in the case of Brex, it was they had worked on a FinTech company in Brazil when they were younger, and so I'm like, "You need to work more on the thing all about and not the thing nothing about." And that was what worked for them. In the case of Retool, it was the same thing. They had built similar internal tools both at their internships as well as for Cashew. They had all these dashboards they built to operate their Venmo competitor. And so they knew a lot about what to build in the case of postprod, pivoting and through idea, they knew a lot about analytics and had strong opinions about it. And so it was much closer than what the original idea is. (00:15:41): In the case of Zip, Rujul knows a lot about a lot of things and he knew a lot about the crazy picture and process at Airbnb because he worked there. A good pivot is like going home. It's warmer, it's closer to something that you... And it never occurred to you that this thing you know all about would be a good idea or maybe you consciously are like, "I don't want to work on this because burnt out on it." Sometimes someone has to get over this barrier they have on why they don't want to work on a certain idea.
turns.zh: 通常，成功的转变会从你所擅长的领域变得更热而不是更冷，并且以某种方式建立在你从先前的想法中学到的东西上。正确的？就 Brex 而言，他们年轻时曾在巴西的一家金融科技公司工作过，所以我想，“你需要在所有事情上投入更多精力，而不是无关紧要的事情。”这对他们来说是有效的。对于 Retool 来说，情况也是一样。他们在实习期间以及为 Cashew 构建了类似的内部工具。他们拥有所有这些仪表板来运营他们的 Venmo 竞争对手。因此，他们非常了解在后期生产、转型和创意方面要构建什么，他们非常了解分析，并对此有强烈的看法。所以它比最初的想法更接近。 (00:15:41)：就 Zip 而言，Rujul 了解很多事情，而且他对 Airbnb 的疯狂图片和流程了解很多，因为他在那里工作。一次好的转向就像回家一样。它更温暖，更接近你的东西……你从来没有想过你所知道的这件事会是一个好主意，或者你可能有意识地想，“我不想做这个，因为它已经精疲力尽了。”有时，有人必须克服他们为什么不想研究某个想法的障碍。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: These are amazing. I like how modest you are. I'm like, "Oh, here's a big idea." And then you just give very tactical items to look for. So essentially a good pivot in your experience is you're getting closer, warmer towards something you have actual experience in, and two, it builds on something you've done. Can be essentially the core idea of a pivot, right? Where you're...
turns.zh: 这些太棒了。我喜欢你的谦虚。我想，“哦，这是一个好主意。”然后你只需提供非常战术性的物品来寻找即可。因此，从本质上讲，你的经历的一个良好的支点是你越来越接近、更热衷于你有实际经历的事情，第二，它建立在你已经做过的事情的基础上。本质上可能是枢轴的核心思想，对吧？你在哪里...

turns.speaker: Dalton Caldwell
turns.en: In the example of Segment, which is obviously a really big successful company, they started with something to tell your professor you were confused in class. It was software that they sold to universities. And then they ended up pivoting to something like a mixed panel competitor after two years and it's because they learned about how analytics works running their first idea, okay? And then no one wanted to adopt their mixed panel competitor. And so they were like, "We should make this JavaScript thing that you embed on your website that can send events to multiple endpoints at the same time so that way people would be willing to try our mixed panel competitor side by side with mixed panels to show that it's better." And then they were like, "Oh yeah, no one actually wants that. They just want this JavaScript to send events to different locations." And so there's no way those founders could have started with the final idea. You get what I mean? (00:17:30): There was no universe where they would've made up the idea for Segment because they didn't know anything about how analytics worked, but because they were grinding for multiple years and became experts on these things is a side effect of their earlier ideas. They ended up with really good unique insights.
turns.zh: 以 Segment 为例，这显然是一家非常成功的大公司，他们首先告诉你的教授你在课堂上感到困惑。他们向大学出售的是软件。然后两年后他们最终转向了混合面板竞争对手之类的东西，这是因为他们了解了分析如何运行他们的第一个想法，好吗？然后没有人愿意采用他们的混合面板竞争对手。所以他们说，“我们应该让这个 JavaScript 东西嵌入到你的网站上，它可以同时将事件发送到多个端点，这样人们就会愿意尝试我们的混合面板竞争对手与混合面板，以证明它更好。”然后他们说，“哦，是的，没有人真正想要这样。他们只是希望这个 JavaScript 将事件发送到不同的位置。”因此，这些创始人不可能从最终的想法开始。你明白我的意思吗？ (00:17:30)：他们不会提出分段的想法，因为他们对分析的工作原理一无所知，但因为他们多年的磨练并成为这些事情的专家，这是他们早期想法的副作用。他们最终获得了非常好的独特见解。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I think that's a really important point there is you don't need to necessarily have that experience before you start the company, could come from trying to build the company.
turns.zh: 我认为这是非常重要的一点，你不一定需要在创办公司之前拥有这种经验，这些经验可能来自于尝试建立公司。

turns.speaker: Dalton Caldwell
turns.en: Exactly.
turns.zh: 确切地。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: A big question people are always wondering is, should I pivot? Is this the time to pivot? Should I keep trying this idea? What's your advice there of just, okay, now you should really be thinking about something else?
turns.zh: 人们总是想知道的一个大问题是，我应该转向吗？现在是转折点的时候了吗？我应该继续尝试这个想法吗？你有什么建议，好吧，现在你真的应该考虑点别的事情吗？

turns.speaker: Dalton Caldwell
turns.en: Again, this is one of those where I like to give very bespoke nuanced advice on a case by case basis to the folks in YC. But again, just to give you a preview of how I would think about it, I would look at how many more ideas the founder has on how to make it grow. If it's not going well and you're out of ideas, that is usually a good time to pivot. But when you have half a dozen or a dozen really good growth ideas that you haven't tried yet, try them. Right? Hey, give it a shot. Again, in the Airbnb story, right? They tried all sorts of stuff including cereal and conventions. They had a bunch of zany ideas on growth and they didn't run out of them. And so I think when there's still gas in the tank on an idea that might be a reason to stay the course. And when literally the founder is like, "Yeah, I don't know, I guess maybe we should pay influencers or something." When that's the kind of ideas they're coming up with, that might be a better sign to pivot.
turns.zh: 同样，这是我喜欢根据具体情况向 YC 的人员提供非常定制的细致建议的地方之一。但同样，为了让你预览一下我的想法，我会看看创始人对于如何让它成长还有多少想法。如果进展不顺利并且你没有想法，这通常是转变的好时机。但是，当你有六六个或十几个非常好的增长想法尚未尝试时，请尝试一下。正确的？嘿，试一试。还是在 Airbnb 的故事中，对吧？他们尝试了各种各样的东西，包括谷物和会议。他们对增长有很多奇特的想法，但他们并没有用完。所以我认为，当一个想法仍有动力时，这可能是坚持到底的理由。当创始人字面意思是，“是的，我不知道，我想也许我们应该付钱给有影响力的人或者其他什么。”当他们提出这样的想法时，这可能是一个更好的转变迹象。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That is incredibly helpful. Coming back to Zip real quick, they went through I think six different pivots before they landed on this idea that is now a billion-dollar business. Is there anything from that specific journey that you found really interesting? Because they went in so many different directions like accounting, marketplaces and-
turns.zh: 这非常有帮助。很快回到 Zip，他们经历了六次不同的转变，然后才找到了这个现在价值十亿美元的业务的想法。在那段特定的旅程中，有什么事情是您觉得真正有趣的吗？因为他们进入了很多不同的方向，比如会计、市场和——

turns.speaker: Dalton Caldwell
turns.en: Yeah. I think in the example of the Zip founders, they were both such great experts and I knew Rujul really well. He actually worked with me at YC as a visiting partner. And so I was really close to Rujul and he had done this marketplace called FlightCar when he was younger, which was raised a series B, it didn't work out, but it was a really cool company. And I had a lot of confidence in his competence on running a business and executing fast and just having great instincts. He really knows the fundamentals and the problem was they weren't as clear on what market to go into, is still with me. And so I actually suggested to do something in their case, again, this is very bespoke, but my suggestion was to start by looking at what companies are publicly traded and/or owned by private equity that are large and that also are hated by their customers, and to try to intentionally find where there's a knowable big market within incumbent combined with the software is horrible. (00:20:29): And they did that. They basically found out about all this procurement software and what the state of the art was and that was the prompt. Again, maybe he told you this, that was basically the process.
turns.zh: 是的。我认为以 Zip 创始人为例，他们都是非常出色的专家，而且我非常了解 Rujul。实际上，他作为访问合伙人在 YC 与我一起工作。所以我和 Rujul 关系非常密切，他年轻时曾做过一个名为 FlightCar 的市场，该公司获得了 B 轮融资，虽然没有成功，但这是一家非常酷的公司。我对他经营业务、快速执行以及敏锐的直觉的能力充满信心。他确实了解基本面，但问题是他们不太清楚要进入哪个市场，这一点仍然困扰着我。所以我实际上建议在他们的情况下做一些事情，这也是非常定制的，但我的建议是首先看看哪些公司是公开交易的和/或由私募股权公司拥有的，这些公司规模很大，而且也被他们的客户讨厌，并试图故意找到现有的已知大市场与软件相结合是可怕的。 (00:20:29)：他们就这么做了。他们基本上了解了所有这些采购软件以及最先进的技术，这就是提示。再说一遍，也许他告诉过你这个，这基本上就是这个过程。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: He did tell me that. I love that example and piece of advice so much. I don't know why more people don't do this. Basically find a large incumbent with very low NPS and try to disrupt them. So straightforward.
turns.zh: 他确实告诉过我这一点。我非常喜欢这个例子和建议。我不知道为什么更多的人不这样做。基本上找到一个 NPS 非常低的大型现有企业并尝试扰乱它们。如此简单。

turns.speaker: Dalton Caldwell
turns.en: Yeah, I mean, I can't promise that works for everyone, but again, in the very bespoke situation with Rujul, it worked really well because he actually knew exactly once he locked in on that prompt, oh man, he ran a masterclass. They did an A-plus job, was really good.
turns.zh: 是的，我的意思是，我不能保证这对每个人都有效，但是，在鲁朱尔的定制情况下，它的效果非常好，因为一旦他锁定了提示，他实际上就知道，天哪，他举办了一场大师班。他们做得非常出色，真的很棒。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Also Lou, his co-founder, credit to him too.
turns.zh: 他的联合创始人卢先生也对他表示赞赏。

turns.speaker: Dalton Caldwell
turns.en: Of course. Sorry. Yeah. We got to give Lou the shout-out. Lou did an amazing job. I just didn't know Lou as well before he did YC. But you're right, we got to give Lou the credit.
turns.zh: 当然。对不起。是的。我们必须向卢大声喊叫。卢做得非常出色。只是在 Lou 加入 YC 之前我不太了解他。但你是对的，我们必须把功劳归功于卢。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I was watching your chat with Michael Seibel talking about pivots and either you or he used this phrase of you want to move towards the mountains in the desert to find the gold of a new startup idea versus the middle of the city. You're unlikely to find gold in the middle of San Francisco. Is there anything along those lines that you can share?
turns.zh: 我正在看你和迈克尔·塞贝尔（Michael Seibel）谈论枢纽的聊天，你或他用了这句话，你想走向沙漠中的山脉，寻找新创业想法的黄金，而不是市中心。在旧金山市中心你不太可能找到黄金。您有什么可以分享的吗？

turns.speaker: Dalton Caldwell
turns.en: Yeah, I think maybe this pertains into what we see from applications and interviews, which is from where I sit seeing everything people apply to YC with and what they interview with and whatnot. People all have the same idea. Basically imagine this, imagine your information consumption where you're listening to the same podcast, wink, wink, you're reading the same people on Twitter, you're reading the same blog post. Basically you have the same information diet of all these other founders and you're friends with all the same people. Does it seem surprising then that you would all end up with similar startup ideas or similar philosophies on what makes a good startup idea? Of course you are. So this is the metaphor on cities is that if you just are following the same principles and have the same information flow into your brain, you're going to come up with the same ideas with everybody else. (00:22:37): And so the prompt here is to try to go more off the beaten path either from your personal experience, like in the case of Brex and Retool or Whatnot. There was no one else trying to build marketplaces for Funko Pops. Go deeper in your own personal interests or experience to find something that just your exact peer wouldn't come up with in exactly the same way. And again, the Zip example, I don't think other people were trying to build wonky procurement software. That was not an idea that we saw much of. And so again, the prompt to people is try to mix up what your information diet is or what areas of expertise you have and mine that well, versus just having all the same thoughts as everybody else. And so again, let me give you one more example. (00:23:24): A few years ago, startups around trucking were super new and fresh because no one was doing them and they worked really well and then it became completely conventional wisdom to do trucking related startups. I'm not trying to diss anyone, but you'll see things that become fashionable really quickly because someone found success in this unfashionable space and then it becomes fashionable.
turns.zh: 是的，我想这可能与我们从申请和面试中看到的情况有关，也就是我看到人们申请 YC 的所有内容以及他们面试的内容等等。人们都有同样的想法。基本上想象一下，想象一下你的信息消费，你正在收听相同的播客，眨眼，眨眼，你在 Twitter 上阅读相同的人，你正在阅读相同的博客文章。基本上，你和所有其他创始人都有相同的信息饮食，而且你和所有同样的人都是朋友。那么，对于如何打造一个好的创业想法，你们最终都会有相似的创业想法或相似的理念，这似乎令人惊讶吗？当然是。所以这就是城市的比喻，如果你遵循相同的原则并且让相同的信息流入你的大脑，你就会想出与其他人相同的想法。 (00:22:37)：所以这里的提示是尝试更多地偏离你的个人经历，比如 Brex 和 Retool 或 Whatnot 的例子。没有其他人试图为 Funko Pops 建立市场。更深入地研究你自己的个人兴趣或经验，找到一些你的同行不会以完全相同的方式提出的东西。再说一遍，以 Zip 为例，我认为其他人并没有试图构建不稳定的采购软件。我们并没有看到太多这样的想法。同样，对人们的提示是尝试将你的信息饮食是什么或者你拥有哪些专业领域并进行挖掘，而不是仅仅拥有与其他人相同的想法。让我再举一个例子。 (00:23:24)：几年前，围绕卡车运输的初创公司是非常新的和新鲜的，因为没有人在做它们，而且它们运作得非常好，然后做卡车运输相关的初创公司就完全成为传统智慧。我并不是想贬低任何人，但你会看到一些东西很快就会变得时尚，因为有人在这个不时尚的领域取得了成功，然后它就变得时尚了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This is a good segue to something I definitely want to spend time on, which is you have this concept of tarpit ideas, which are essentially ideas people all gravitate towards and get stuck in and either pivot into and then can't pivot out of or try to pivot out of. And essentially it's just consistently bad startup ideas that people continue to try to start. Can you just talk about this and then what is examples of just bad startup ideas that people should stop trying to start?
turns.zh: 这是我绝对想花时间做的事情的一个很好的延续，这就是你有这种柏油思想的概念，这些思想本质上是人们都被吸引并陷入其中的想法，要么转向，然后无法转向，要么试图转向。从本质上讲，人们不断尝试开始的只是一贯糟糕的创业想法。您能简单谈谈这个问题吗？那么人们应该停止尝试的糟糕创业想法有哪些例子呢？

turns.speaker: Dalton Caldwell
turns.en: For people that are familiar with this terminology from us, sometimes they get defensive and don't get what we were saying. By definition it is only a tarpit if it seems like it's not. If it's just a regular idea that is hard, that is not a tarpit. The weird aspect of what we call a tarpit idea is an idea that a lot of people come up with and then it seems like an unsolved problem and you get lots of positive feedback for. Right? And you have a really good set of arguments that it's a really good startup idea. And that's different than a bad startup idea. Do you get what I'm trying to say? A bad startup idea is, I don't know, something that is obviously bad or something where you just can't get any positive feedback on. But some of the most common tarpit would be something like building an app to coordinate with your friends to decide where to go out at night or where to meet up with people, which is really, it's coming from a good place. It's a good idea. (00:25:10): If you ask your friends, "Hey, would you like an app for us to coordinate to hang out more so we can be friends?" They're like, "Yeah, I would love that." You'll get all this positive feedback from the world. And man, people have been starting that startup since the '90s and so you can validate it. Part of being a true tarpit is that you can get good initial validation. Do you get what I mean? And so anyway. And honestly I worked on tarpit ideas myself as a founder, which is a music discovery. This is something I did in my first startup. Music startups are hard and trying to be like, "Oh, we're going to fix music discovery." This was classic things where you can get lots of positive feedback and even get users to work on those things, but there are aspects of it that make it a very hard idea. So does that make sense?
turns.zh: 对于熟悉我们这个术语的人来说，有时他们会采取防御态度，不明白我们在说什么。根据定义，它只是一个柏油坑，如果它看起来不是的话。如果这只是一个很难的常规想法，那它就不是柏油坑。我们所说的“柏油坑想法”的奇怪之处在于，很多人都提出了这个想法，然后它似乎是一个未解决的问题，并且你得到了很多积极的反馈。正确的？你有一系列非常好的论据证明这是一个非常好的创业想法。这与糟糕的创业想法不同。你明白我想说的吗？我不知道，一个糟糕的创业想法是指那些明显不好的想法，或者是你无法得到任何积极反馈的想法。但一些最常见的 tarpit 是像构建一个应用程序来与你的朋友协调来决定晚上去哪里或在哪里与人见面，这确实是一个好地方。这是个好主意。 (00:25:10)：如果你问你的朋友，“嘿，你想要一个应用程序来协调我们更多地出去玩，这样我们就可以成为朋友吗？”他们会说，“是的，我会喜欢的。”您将从世界上得到所有这些积极的反馈。伙计，人们从 20 世纪 90 年代就开始创办这家公司，所以你可以验证它。成为真正的 tarpit 的一部分是您可以获得良好的初始验证。你明白我的意思吗？无论如何。老实说，作为创始人，我自己也致力于沥青坑的想法，这是一种音乐发现。这是我在第一次创业时所做的事情。音乐初创公司很难，并试图表现出“哦，我们要解决音乐发现问题”。这是经典的事情，你可以获得很多积极的反馈，甚至让用户去做这些事情，但它的某些方面使它成为一个非常困难的想法。那么这有道理吗？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Absolutely. I'm also guilty of this. I had this startup called Localmind that allowed you to talk to people, check-in in various locations around the city, on Foursquare and Google back in the day and asked them, "How's it going?" And everyone when they used it, they're like, "Holy shit, this is the most incredible thing I've ever seen. I could see what's happening at this bar that I'm about to go to." And then they never use it again.
turns.zh: 绝对地。我对此也有罪。我有一家名为 Localmind 的初创公司，它允许你与人们交谈，在城市的各个地点、Foursquare 和 Google 上签到，然后问他们，“进展如何？”每个人在使用它时都会说，“天哪，这是我见过的最不可思议的事情。我可以看到我要去的这个酒吧里发生了什么。”然后他们就再也没有使用过它。

turns.speaker: Dalton Caldwell
turns.en: Do you remember when Foursquare clones was all anyone worked on for-
turns.zh: 你还记得吗，当 Foursquare 克隆成为所有人的工作目标时——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Dalton Caldwell
turns.en: Years?
turns.zh: 年？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: They told us Foursquare is going to own this. There's no way this idea you're building is going to be its own thing. And now, yeah, Foursquare is a B2B business.
turns.zh: 他们告诉我们 Foursquare 将拥有这个。你正在构建的这个想法不可能成为它自己的东西。现在，Foursquare 是一家 B2B 企业。

turns.speaker: Dalton Caldwell
turns.en: Yeah. And all the Foursquare clones, if they didn't pivot out of doing what they're doing, wouldn't have worked. So anyway, that's a tarpit, is just something that's super appealing and a lot of people do it. And then you can get validation and that's why is a tarpit, is it draws you in and you get stuck because it seems like it's a good idea and you get all this positive feedback.
turns.zh: 是的。所有的 Foursquare 克隆产品，如果不放弃他们正在做的事情，就不会成功。所以无论如何，那是一个柏油坑，是非常有吸引力的东西，很多人都这样做。然后你就可以得到验证，这就是为什么会有柏油坑，它会吸引你，然后你就会陷入困境，因为这似乎是个好主意，你会得到所有这些积极的反馈。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Along these lines, I was talking to a founder recently and she's asking me, "What causes an investor to say no to you when you're trying to raise money from them?" And I know every investor has a very different perspective on what turns them off to a startup, but is there anything that you find is just like, here, if you do these things, investors will say no.
turns.zh: 沿着这些思路，我最近与一位创始人交谈，她问我：“当你试图从投资者那里筹集资金时，是什么原因导致他们拒绝你？”我知道每个投资者对于是什么让他们对初创公司失去兴趣都有不同的看法，但是你会发现有什么事情就像，在这里，如果你做了这些事情，投资者会说不。

turns.speaker: Dalton Caldwell
turns.en: Maybe my best advice here is for founders to put themselves in the shoes of investors and just imagine what their life is like and how if you are in their shoes you would make decisions. And so given this framework, a lot of investors just don't make that many investments and as per what we talked about earlier, life is short. And so there's lots of things that an investor that in their hearts thinks it is pretty good and they're like, "Oh, I like this person and I like their pitch, but I only am going to do a few investments. And so even though I really like a lot about this, I'm going to say no." And I often think that founders think that there's some secret truth that's being held from them on why someone says no or they want more feedback. "I need feedback." That's like, well, the feedback is we didn't want to invest and it really is just that. (00:28:05): And so I think if you put yourself in the shoes of an investor of like, "Hey, I only could do a few of these a year, I have very limited budget." They're really just trying to pick the things that they're either personally most excited about or things that they think can be truly phenomenally big in some way. Or again, I know you do investments too, so it's that you only get so many shots as an investor. And so anything that doesn't seem like this is the one, this is the one I want to do is a no. And that that's actually why they're saying no versus, "Oh, you had a bad zoom setup or something. Oh, we didn't like what color your shirt was. We said no." I don't think that's how this actually works.
turns.zh: 也许我在这里最好的建议是，创始人将自己置于投资者的立场上，想象他们的生活是什么样的，以及如果你处于他们的立场上，你会如何做出决定。因此，考虑到这个框架，很多投资者只是不会进行那么多投资，而且根据我们之前谈到的，生命是短暂的。因此，有很多事情是投资者内心认为这非常好的事情，他们会说，“哦，我喜欢这个人，我喜欢他们的推销，但我只会做一些投资。所以即使我真的很喜欢这个，我也会说不。”我经常认为，创始人认为他们隐瞒了一些秘密真相，说明为什么有人拒绝或他们想要更多反馈。 “我需要反馈。”这就像，嗯，反馈是我们不想投资，事实就是这样。 (00:28:05)：所以我认为如果你把自己放在投资者的立场上，“嘿，我一年只能做其中的一些，我的预算非常有限。”他们实际上只是想选择他们个人最兴奋的事情，或者他们认为在某种程度上可能真正非常大的事情。或者再说一次，我知道你也做投资，所以作为投资者你只能得到这么多机会。所以任何看起来不是我想要做的事情都是不。这实际上就是为什么他们说“不”，而不是“哦，你的变焦设置不好或什么的。哦，我们不喜欢你衬衫的颜色。我们说不。”我不认为这实际上是这样的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I think that's such a good piece of advice that it's not necessarily they don't believe in what you're doing, it's they have better options and they're waiting for something that hits the higher bar because they have a lot of options.
turns.zh: 我认为这是一个很好的建议，他们不一定不相信你正在做的事情，而是他们有更好的选择，他们正在等待达到更高标准的东西，因为他们有很多选择。

turns.speaker: Dalton Caldwell
turns.en: Yeah. Because again, if you ask someone or put yourself in the investor's shoes, wouldn't you be making decisions the same way? Usually founders are like, "Yeah." If you do that exercise, a lot of this starts to make way more sense.
turns.zh: 是的。因为，如果你询问某人或将自己置于投资者的立场上，你不会以同样的方式做出决定吗？通常创始人都会说“是的”。如果你做了这个练习，很多事情就会变得更有意义。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Specifically when you're evaluating startups. I wasn't going to go into this, but I think it might be interesting, is market size. How do you think about the importance of large TAM as an investor YC?
turns.zh: 特别是当你评估初创公司时。我本来不打算讨论这个问题，但我认为这可能很有趣，那就是市场规模。您如何看待大TAM作为YC投资人的重要性？

turns.speaker: Dalton Caldwell
turns.en: I think it really depends on what stage you're investing at and it's absolutely critical the later stage you get. Right? If you're going to invest in a very high valuation, it is really important. The earlier you go, the less it matters. And some of the most phenomenally good startups, if you were really pedantic about it, the TAM would be tiny. The TAM of Uber would be nothing, right? The TAM of Airbnb would've been nothing. TI funded Razorpay, which is I think the largest payment processor in India, and the TAM of that was tiny because no one was using credit cards in 2015 in India. So you had to believe that the size of the credit card industry in India would 100X. Well, guess what happened? You know what I'm saying? So I'm not saying that having a large market someday doesn't matter, of course it does eventually. But trying to be super pedantic about market size when it's a pre-seed company or someone applying to YC, it's just not something I'd put a lot of thought. (00:30:34): And again, Whatnot. What's the TAM of the collectible Funko Pop industry? I don't know. I don't think it's that big, man. I don't know if you did that analysis when you invested, but I think is pretty small, but I wasn't worried about it. That was the last thing I was worried about.
turns.zh: 我认为这实际上取决于您在哪个阶段进行投资，并且在您所处的后期阶段绝对至关重要。正确的？如果你要投资一个非常高的估值，这一点真的很重要。走得越早，事情就越不重要。对于一些最出色的初创公司来说，如果你真的很迂腐的话，TAM 就会很小。 Uber 的 TAM 就什么都不是了，对吧？ Airbnb 的 TAM 就什么也不是了。 TI 资助了 Razorpay，我认为这是印度最大的支付处理商，其 TAM 很小，因为 2015 年印度没有人使用信用卡。所以你必须相信印度信用卡行业的规模将扩大 100 倍。好吧，猜猜发生了什么？你知道我在说什么吗？所以我并不是说有一天拥有一个大市场并不重要，当然最终会重要。但当它是一家前种子公司或申请 YC 的人时，我不会对市场规模过于迂腐，我不会花很多心思。 (00:30:34)：再说一遍，什么。 Funko Pop 收藏品行业的 TAM 是多少？我不知道。我不认为它有那么大，伙计。我不知道你投资的时候有没有做过这样的分析，但我认为这个分析很小，但我并不担心。这是我最后担心的事情。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It makes so much sense that at YC you don't think about it that much because of, as you said, many startups pivot anyway. So if you like the team-
turns.zh: 这很有意义，在 YC，你不会考虑太多，因为正如你所说，许多初创公司无论如何都会转向。所以如果你喜欢这个团队-

turns.speaker: Dalton Caldwell
turns.en: Yeah. And I'm not saying it's not important, it's not... And the things I'm worried about is like, hey, how do you get users? Hey, how do you grow? Things like that. Are you making something people want? Those are the things I'm really worried about as opposed to, ooh, I ran an Excel model and I'm worried this might not be a big enough TAM. That's not the top of my list.
turns.zh: 是的。我并不是说这不重要，这不是……我担心的事情是，嘿，你如何获得用户？嘿嘿，你怎么成长啊？诸如此类的事情。你在做人们想要的东西吗？这些是我真正担心的事情，而不是，哦，我运行了一个 Excel 模型，我担心这可能不是一个足够大的 TAM。这不是我的首要任务。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I think it's important to acknowledge that a lot of investors are very... YC I think is unique in a lot of ways where you invest very early and you help people through this journey. A lot of investors are very focused on TAM, so you may find you're getting turned down because they don't think there's a big enough market for you to build a big business, right?
turns.zh: 我认为重要的是要承认很多投资者都非常……我认为 YC 在很多方面都是独一无二的，你很早就进行投资，并帮助人们度过这一旅程。很多投资者都非常关注 TAM，所以你可能会发现你被拒绝了，因为他们认为没有足够大的市场让你建立一个大企业，对吧？

turns.speaker: Dalton Caldwell
turns.en: Yeah. Or that you're asking them to believe a crazy leap of faith that, again, they could say, "Well, it's theoretically possible you'll be able to sell more than Funko Pops, and I understand that that is your pitch, but I have other opportunities that are less risky." You know what I'm saying? A lot of founders make the argument that the TAM is big, and you can say, "Wow, that's a really interesting argument and I'm not going to argue with you about it, but no, I'm not going to..." And so again, it's hard to get someone to engage in a debate about TAM even if you have some proof points. Ultimately, a lot of investors just don't like that risk. Fair enough.
turns.zh: 是的。或者你要求他们相信一个疯狂的信念，他们可能会说，“好吧，理论上你的销量可能会超过 Funko Pops，我明白这是你的想法，但我还有其他风险较小的机会。”你知道我在说什么吗？很多创始人都认为 TAM 很大，你可以说，“哇，这是一个非常有趣的论点，我不会和你争论这个问题，但是不，我不会……”所以，即使你有一些证据，也很难让人们参与关于 TAM 的辩论。最终，许多投资者就是不喜欢这种风险。很公平。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Fair enough. Going in a slightly different direction. So someone else that worked with you, another Lenny, Lenny Bogdonoff who started a company called Milk, and then he was head of growth at OpenAI for a bit. He asked me to ask you about things product leaders and startups should watch out for. Does that ring a bell?
turns.zh: 很公平。朝着稍微不同的方向前进。与你一起工作的另一个人，另一个 Lenny，Lenny Bogdonoff，他创办了一家名为 Milk 的公司，然后他在 OpenAI 担任过一段时间的增长主管。他让我问你产品领导者和初创公司应该注意的事情。这是否敲响了警钟？

turns.speaker: Dalton Caldwell
turns.en: I don't remember the specific office hours, but I understand the question and I of course remember Lenny. I think that the advice that he's referencing here is just how important it is to not overdelegate and for the founders to stay close to things, as well as watch out for the trap of hiring super senior people with fancy resumes, really early in a startup. I think that's what he's referencing there. And again, this is definitely one of those very basic things that we find ourselves repeating a lot where they're like, "Yeah, yeah, I get it. Don't overdelegate. We get it, Dalton." And then two years later they're like, "Wow, we overdelegated. We need to go clean that up." So that is probably the best product advice. And the folks that are really great at product, the founders that are always deeply in the weeds on product and still care a lot and are still talking to customers, no matter how late stage it gets, again, I'm sure you experienced this in Airbnb culture, but you can't delegate caring about your users and you can't delegate caring that the product is great. That is so critical.
turns.zh: 我不记得具体的办公时间，但我明白这个问题，我当然记得莱尼。我认为他在这里引用的建议是，不要过度授权，创始人要密切关注事情，并提防在初创公司的早期雇用简历精美的超级高级人才的陷阱。我认为这就是他所指的内容。再说一次，这绝对是我们经常重复的非常基本的事情之一，他们会说，“是的，是的，我明白了。不要过度授权。我们明白了，道尔顿。”两年后，他们会说，“哇，我们授权过度了。我们需要清理这个问题。”所以这可能是最好的产品建议。那些真正擅长产品的人，那些总是深入研究产品的创始人，无论发展到多晚，仍然非常关心并仍在与客户交谈，我相信你在 Airbnb 文化中也经历过这种情况，但你不能把对用户的关心委托给他人，也不能把对产品的关心委托给他人。这非常关键。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: To make this even more real, what is it that you see them do? It's they hire a PM too early, they hire a senior salesperson too early, what are the-
turns.zh: 更真实的是，你看到他们做了什么？是他们太早聘用了产品经理，他们太早聘用了高级销售人员，这些是什么——

turns.speaker: Dalton Caldwell
turns.en: Yeah, I think that you get pushed often by investors to hire executives or to scale the team or you raise all this money, you got to spend it, you got to show you're serious about growth and building a world-class organization, whatever, stuff like that. And so you end up with super nice people with super shiny resumes from big tech companies. "Oh wow, they did this amazing thing at Google." And then they hire them and then you wake up one day and you're like, "Oh wow, everything went wrong." It's not really anyone's fault, it's just that you took your eye off the ball and this is what happens to first-time founders a lot.
turns.zh: 是的，我认为你经常被投资者催促去雇用高管或扩大团队规模，或者你筹集所有这些钱，你必须花掉它，你必须表明你对增长和建立世界级组织的认真态度，诸如此类的事情。所以你最终会得到来自大型科​​技公司的超级好人，拥有超级闪亮的简历。 “哇哦，他们在谷歌做了一件了不起的事情。”然后他们雇佣了他们，然后有一天你醒来，你会想，“哦，哇，一切都出了问题。”这并不是任何人的错，只是你把注意力从球上移开了，这就是首次创始人经常遇到的情况。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: How do you as a founder then have time to do all these things? Is there any guidance you give just like don't overdelegate, don't over hire? But also, you have 24 hours in a day? Is it just find the time, prioritize well, or is there more to it?
turns.zh: 作为创始人，您如何有时间做所有这些事情？您是否提供了任何指导，例如不要过度授权，不要过度雇用？而且，你一天有24小时吗？是只是找到时间，分清轻重缓急，还是还有更多的事情要做？

turns.speaker: Dalton Caldwell
turns.en: I think if you just care a lot about your customers and you care a lot about the product, your instincts are pretty good on what to spend time on. And so for example, spending tons and tons of time hanging out with investors and networking, it's probably the thing that I would be cutting. You know what I'm saying? It's what we talked about earlier. If you really love what you're doing, no one needs to tell you how to reprioritize your time. Your intuition will be correct on what you should be spending all your time on, which is being obsessed with product.
turns.zh: 我认为，如果你非常关心你的客户并且非常关心产品，你的直觉就会很好地知道应该花时间在什么地方。例如，花费大量时间与投资者和人际交往，这可能是我要削减的事情。你知道我在说什么吗？这就是我们之前谈到的。如果你真的热爱你正在做的事情，没有人需要告诉你如何重新安排你的时间。你的直觉是正确的，你应该把所有的时间花在什么事情上，那就是对产品的痴迷。

turns.speaker: Dalton Caldwell
turns.en: I completely agree with what Gustav said, but to look at this from a different frame, I think is that the founders lose hope. And when you and your heart is like, "Yeah, we're failing." (00:38:17): And so it's pretty rare, I would argue, that the cause of death is that they had lots of firepower and they were feeling really positive and they just ran out of money. That's actually more rare than founders think. It's much more common that they still have some money left. I'm not saying a lot, but some money and they're just like, "Yeah, I'm done. turns.zh: 我完全同意古斯塔夫所说的，但从不同的角度来看，我认为是创始人失去了希望。当你和你的心说：“是的，我们失败了。”当我与创始人会面时，当他们承认自己失败时，我可以看到这一点。第一种情况是，“我们还有一次行动。我们还有一次尝试。”当他们觉得有更多的想法或者有一些最后的万福玛丽的事情时，你可以从他们的眼睛里看到。它并不总是有效，但几乎就像你必须不接受你会失败。只要你不接受这种情况将会发生，通常你可以采取更多措施来拯救公司。也许是为了盈利，也许是为了做一些其他滑稽的事情，也许是为了推出新产品。 (00:38:17)：我认为，这种情况很少见，因为他们拥有大量火力，而且他们感觉非常积极，但他们的钱用完了。这实际上比创始人想象的更为罕见。更常见的是，他们还剩下一些钱。我没说太多，只是给了一些钱，然后他们就说，“是的，我已经完成了。我没有主意了。我不想再这样做了。”再说一次，这很公平。但你明白我在说什么吗？我认为创始人担心他们会耗尽资金，这就是他们要倒闭的原因。更常见的是，他们的想法行不通，他们与联合创始人发生了激烈的争吵，然后他们无法就工作内容达成一致，然后他们就说：“我不想再这样做了。”他们就关门了。这是最常见的死亡原因，听起来就像那个故事。

turns.en: Collison Install.

turns.speaker: Dalton Caldwell
turns.en: The Collison Install is what often happens with customers, is that they say, "Yes, I want you buy your product." And then they do not implement it, they just go quiet. There's no implementation and this is very bad if you're selling software to someone. If they never implement it, they're going to churn. You basically failed on the one yard line, okay? And so they developed this tactic to be like, "Oh, well, I'm at the neighborhood, I'll drop by your office to help you implement Stripe and just create..." Again, it was a little awkward like we talked about earlier, but you would be like, "Yeah. I'm in the neighborhood. How about I drop by?" And then they would show up and they'd be like, "Cool, cool. Can pull up your text editor?" "Oh yeah, cool. All right." "Hey, can I drive? Can I have the keyboard?" (00:46:43): And they would just install Stripe into the customer's website, smiling, being charming guys. And they'd be like, "Oh, that's cool. Okay. Well, can we roll out the website now?" And they basically would not go away until you finish the implementation of Stripe. And again, it was actually helpful because they were doing all this white glove service to get it implemented. That was very effective. And I think the takeaway from that story is even when you get a yes, you're not actually done with sales. You have to finish the last mile to get the thing implemented. And they were very good at that.
turns.zh: 科里森安装是客户经常遇到的情况，他们会说：“是的，我希望你购买你的产品。”然后他们不实施它，他们只是保持沉默。没有实施，如果你向某人出售软件，这是非常糟糕的。如果他们从不实施它，他们就会流失。你基本上在一码线上失败了，好吗？所以他们制定了这样的策略，“哦，好吧，我在附近，我会去你的办公室帮助你实施 Stripe 并创建......”同样，这有点尴尬，就像我们之前谈到的，但你会说，“是的。我在附近。我顺便去一下怎么样？”然后他们就会出现，他们会说，“酷，酷。可以打开你的文本编辑器吗？” “哦，是的，很酷。好吧。” “嘿，我可以开车吗？可以给我键盘吗？” (00:46:43)：他们只是将 Stripe 安装到客户的网站上，面带微笑，表现得很有魅力。他们会说，“哦，那很酷。好吧。那么，我们现在可以推出该网站吗？”在你完成 Stripe 的实现之前，它们基本上不会消失。再说一次，这实际上很有帮助，因为他们正在提供所有这些白手套服务来实现它。这非常有效。我认为这个故事的要点是，即使你得到了肯定，你实际上还没有完成销售。你必须完成最后一英里才能实现这一目标。他们非常擅长这一点。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That was an incredible story. And now they're, I don't know, a hundred billion in business and that's how it all begins.
turns.zh: 那是一个令人难以置信的故事。现在，我不知道，他们的业务已达到一千亿美元，这就是一切的开始。

turns.speaker: Dalton Caldwell
turns.en: Yeah. I was an early Stripe customer at my startup and yeah, Patrick would... We used Google Talk at the time. Patrick would be sending me messages on a weekly basis just checking in. And so again, it's funny how successful these folks get, but yeah, Patrick was very hands-on with all of his customers and was extremely available. I can say that because I was one of them. Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。我是我初创公司的早期 Stripe 客户，是的，Patrick 会...我们当时使用 Google Talk。帕特里克每周都会向我发送消息，只是检查一下。同样，这些人取得的成功很有趣，但是，是的，帕特里克对他的所有客户都非常亲力亲为，而且非常乐意帮助。我可以这么说，因为我就是其中之一。是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And I'm sure he had social anxiety going through all that. That wasn't a comfortable thing to do, just keep pushing people to install your software and deploy.
turns.zh: 我确信他经历了这一切，患有社交焦虑症。这不是一件舒服的事情，只是不断地推动人们安装和部署你的软件。

turns.speaker: Dalton Caldwell
turns.en: Oh, surely not. If you want your startup to work, this is just what you got to do. Comes with the territory.
turns.zh: 哦，当然不是。如果你想让你的初创公司成功，这就是你必须要做的。随领土而来。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This is going to be just a way broad question and I don't know if you'll have an answer, but just are there other just patterns you find across startups that do well? This is maybe the $64 million question of just founders and what they do that ends up leading to success.
turns.zh: 这将是一个非常广泛的问题，我不知道您是否会有答案，但是您是否在初创公司中发现了其他表现良好的模式？这也许是一个价值 6400 万美元的问题，只涉及创始人以及他们所做的事情最终会带来成功。

turns.speaker: Dalton Caldwell
turns.en: I don't think personality types matter as much. I've seen very quiet people, very extroverted people. You name it. I've seen all sorts of personality types. So for me personally, I don't think there's a personality type that people should copy and be like, "I need to be like this person. I need to be Steve Jobs. I need to be Elon." I don't really believe in that because there's just so much variation. Tony from DoorDash is so different than a lot of folks, and Rujul is so different and Grant from Whatnot. These are all very, very different people. Patrick is a different kind of person. Ryan from Flexport. These are just very different personality types. But the thing that I would argue folks that build really big companies have in common is they just really want it and they really believe in themselves and they really believe they can make it work. And that they're somehow deep in their internal psyche, there's something that's like, "I'm the one and I won't accept this not working." (00:49:26): And even though objectively there's all this data coming in, this isn't working, this is bad. My employees want to quit, my executives want to quit. Whatever it is. Somewhere deep down in there, they're like, "Oh yeah, I'm going to make this work. This company is going to be big." And they just believe. And it's almost like that internal gravitational force inside of them is so large, it warps the world to bend to that will. And people start to believe it because they believe it so much and they convince their employees to believe in and they convince everyone around them that this is going to happen for them. And so again, this is not a personality trait. I'm arguing this is a core belief.
turns.zh: 我不认为性格类型那么重要。我见过非常安静的人，非常外向的人。你说出它的名字。我见过各种各样的性格类型。因此，就我个人而言，我不认为人们应该效仿某种性格类型，比如“我需要像这个人。我需要成为史蒂夫·乔布斯。我需要成为埃隆。”我不太相信这一点，因为差异太大了。 DoorDash 的托尼与很多人都非常不同，Rujul 和 Whatnot 的格兰特也非常不同。这些都是非常非常不同的人。帕特里克是一个不同类型的人。来自 Flexport 的 Ryan。这些只是非常不同的性格类型。但我认为，创建真正大公司的人有一个共同点，那就是他们真的想要它，他们真的相信自己，他们真的相信自己可以让它发挥作用。他们在内心深处有一种感觉，“我就是那个人，我不会接受这不起作用。” (00:49:26)：尽管客观上有所有这些数据进来，但这不起作用，这很糟糕。我的员工想辞职，我的高管想辞职。不管是什么。在内心深处，他们会想，“哦，是的，我会让这件事成功。这家公司会变得很大。”他们只是相信。就好像它们内部的引力是如此之大，它扭曲了世界以使其屈服于这种意志。人们开始相信这一点，因为他们非常相信这一点，他们说服员工相信，他们让周围的每个人相信这将会发生在他们身上。再说一次，这不是一种人格特质。我认为这是一个核心信念。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So interesting. And it connects so much to what we've been talking about. Just don't die. Don't lose hope in what you're working on. A founder hearing this might feel like, "Man, I don't know if I'm so convinced this is going to work." In your experience, how much of this is internally, they're so certain and convinced versus externally, they need to show this confidence?
turns.zh: 太有趣了。它与我们一直在谈论的内容有很大的联系。只是别死。不要对你正在做的事情失去希望。创始人听到这句话可能会觉得，“伙计，我不知道我是否确信这会起作用。”根据您的经验，其中有多少是内部的，他们如此确定和确信，与外部相比，他们需要表现出这种信心？

turns.speaker: Dalton Caldwell
turns.en: Well, I think it's internally they're convinced. Yeah, I'm not sure it's external. But, and this is the big but, no one has this at the early stages when they don't have a good idea and they don't have customers and it's objectively not working. And so again, I know a lot of founders are like, "Well, I don't feel that way. Oh no, maybe I'm an imposter and I shouldn't do a startup." Well, of course you don't feel that way if you haven't talked to any customers and haven't built a product. But what usually happens is you pivot to a good idea where you start with a good idea that you care about and customers you care about and you launch it. And the better the product does, the more obsessed you get with your own company. (00:51:12): I think in the case of Stripe, I don't want to tell Patrick's story for him, but I recall him saying at some point he wasn't as sure that Stripe was going to work until they were a year or two in. And then once it started working and then they really believed in it. But it wasn't like he woke up one day and like, "Stripe is the thing. It's going to work." I think you build conviction and you have this network effect virtual cycle where you get work conviction. The more customers reflect back to you and data reflects back to you that you're on the right track.
turns.zh: 嗯，我认为他们内心是相信的。是的，我不确定它是外部的。但是，这是一个大问题，没有人在早期阶段拥有这个，因为他们没有一个好主意，也没有客户，而且客观上不起作用。再说一次，我知道很多创始人都会说，“好吧，我不这么认为。哦，不，也许我是个冒名顶替者，我不应该创业。”好吧，如果你没有与任何客户交谈并且没有构建产品，你当然不会有这种感觉。但通常发生的情况是，你转向一个好主意，从你关心的好主意和你关心的客户开始，然后推出它。产品做得越好，你就越痴迷于自己的公司。 (00:51:12)：我认为就 Stripe 而言，我不想为他讲述 Patrick 的故事，但我记得他曾说过，在他们工作一两年之前，他并不确定 Stripe 是否会发挥作用。一旦它开始发挥作用，他们就真的相信了它。但他并不是有一天一觉醒来就说：“条纹就是重点。它会起作用的。”我认为你建立了信念，你就有了这个网络效应的虚拟循环，你可以在其中获得工作信念。越多的客户向您反映，数据向您反映，您正走在正确的道路上。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This is exactly what Scott Belsky shared in our episode when I asked him when to pivot is, do you have more conviction this is going to work or less conviction over time? And so I like that connection we just made there. Okay, so we've talked about all these way startups fail, bad ideas, tarpit ideas. I want to go to the flip side and talk about good startup ideas. So recently you put out a request for startups, which is essentially 20 categories of ideas that you want to fund, that YC wants to fund. Can you share some of these ideas that you're excited about? And basically you're looking to fund and looking for founders to work on.
turns.zh: 这正是斯科特·贝尔斯基（Scott Belsky）在我们的节目中分享的内容，当我问他何时转向时，随着时间的推移，你是否更有信心这会起作用，还是越来越不那么有信心？所以我喜欢我们刚刚在那里建立的联系。好的，我们已经讨论了初创公司失败的所有方式，糟糕的想法，柏油想法。我想从另一方面谈谈好的创业想法。最近，您向初创公司提出了一个要求，这基本上是您想要资助、YC 希望资助的 20 类创意。您能分享一些您感到兴奋的想法吗？基本上，你正在寻找资金并寻找创始人来工作。

turns.speaker: Dalton Caldwell
turns.en: Yeah. And so we put out the request for startups just to inspire people to maybe apply with ideas that aren't the ones that we always see. It's not prescriptive like we will only fund ideas on this list. It is not that at all. Remember what I talked about earlier with information diet? We're trying to mix up some of the information diet about what kind of ideas people might be contemplating. There aren't currently. And so a couple of the ones that we put out there, I made one about ERPs which is enterprise resource planning software. And I did that because I get so few applications on that and they're usually pretty good. And I just would love to see more people look at that and learn about what the ERPs are, just because it's so rare that people apply with that. And now I have a feeling we're going to see a lot more applications working on that. And so it worked as intended, which is to introduce this idea space to founders that didn't even know what an ERP was. Now they'll go learn about it. (00:53:16): Another one is we'd like to fund open source companies. And so that's one of the RFSs where if more people apply to YC with open ideas, I think we'd be pretty excited about that. Maybe founders didn't realize that that would be something we want to fund. Same with space companies. Yeah, we've had a lot of success with space companies. Several of the folks that are actually going to space right now that aren't SpaceX or YC companies. And so I think sometimes founders feel like those ideas are too bold and ambitious, but no, I'd love if more people apply with space companies. And so think about it that way, where we're trying to put out of idea spaces that perhaps someone subconsciously filtered out as what might be a good startup idea. And hopefully that creates a new set of startup ideation for the person.
turns.zh: 是的。因此，我们向初创公司提出了要求，只是为了激励人们应用一些我们不常看到的想法。这并不是规定性的，就像我们只会资助这个清单上的想法一样。根本不是那样的。还记得我之前谈到的信息饮食吗？我们正在尝试混合一些有关人们可能正在考虑的想法的信息。目前没有。因此，在我们发布的几款软件中，我制作了一款关于 ERP 的软件，即企业资源规划软件。我这样做是因为我收到的申请很少，而且通常都很好。我只是希望看到更多的人关注这一点并了解 ERP 是什么，因为很少有人申请它。现在我有一种感觉，我们将看到更多的应用程序致力于此。所以它按预期发挥作用，即将这个想法空间介绍给甚至不知道 ERP 是什么的创始人。现在他们要去了解一下。 (00:53:16)：另一个问题是我们愿意资助开源公司。这就是 RFS 之一，如果更多人以开放的想法申请 YC，我想我们会对此感到非常兴奋。也许创始人没有意识到这将是我们想要资助的事情。航天公司也是如此。是的，我们在航天公司方面取得了很多成功。现在有几个真正要去太空的人不是 SpaceX 或 YC 公司。因此，我认为有时创始人会觉得这些想法过于大胆和雄心勃勃，但不，如果有更多的人申请太空公司，我会很高兴。因此，以这种方式思考，我们试图排除可能有人下意识地过滤掉的想法空间，因为这可能是一个好的创业想法。希望这能为人们创造一套新的创业理念。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And we're going to link to this page in the show notes for folks that want to explore. I'll give a couple more real quick. A way to end cancer, no big deal. Spatial computing, new defense technology, bringing manufacturing back to America. So a lot of hard science, deep tech stuff, which is maybe a new... I don't know. I imagine you guys have invested this in the past, but it feels like trend.
turns.zh: 我们将在节目笔记中为想要探索的人们提供指向此页面的链接。我会很快再给几个。一种结束癌症的方法，没什么大不了的。空间计算、新的国防技术，将制造业带回美国。很多硬科学、深科技的东西，这可能是新的……我不知道。我想你们过去也投资过这个，但感觉像是一种趋势。

turns.speaker: Dalton Caldwell
turns.en: We totally have, right? So these aren't like, "Oh, we've never invested in these before." It's more of like, "Hey, it'd be cool if we saw more applications along these lines." It would be nice because it currently feels a little bit under... There could be more startups working on this stuff.
turns.zh: 我们完全有，对吧？所以这些不像，“哦，我们以前从未投资过这些。”它更像是，“嘿，如果我们看到更多类似的应用程序，那就太酷了。”那就太好了，因为目前感觉有点不足……可能会有更多的初创公司致力于这方面的工作。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, instead of the tarpit ideas. A couple more real quick, better enterprise glue.
turns.zh: 是的，而不是柏油坑的想法。一些更快速、更好的企业粘合剂。

turns.speaker: Dalton Caldwell
turns.en: Yeah, I like that idea.
turns.zh: 是的，我喜欢这个主意。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Say more about that. What does that look like?
turns.zh: 多说一点吧。那看起来像什么？

turns.speaker: Dalton Caldwell
turns.en: The software to connect all these business systems is usually pretty brittle and janky, and there's been lots of good startups founded to solve this problem. I think there's still a lot more room for improvement and likely LLMs will improve. We'll probably be able to create better and better glue so all sorts of software systems can talk to each other. And so again, very broad idea. But yeah, I think we'll see a lot of very successful companies where that's the kernel of the idea they start with.
turns.zh: 连接所有这些业务系统的软件通常非常脆弱且不稳定，并且已经有许多优秀的初创公司成立来解决这个问题。我认为还有很多改进的空间，法学硕士可能会有所改进。我们可能能够创造出越来越好的粘合剂，以便各种软件系统可以相互通信。再说一遍，这是一个非常广泛的想法。但是，是的，我认为我们会看到很多非常成功的公司，这就是他们开始的想法的核心。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. One last one. Small fine tune models as an alternative to gigantic generic ones. Yeah. Sweet. And so we'll include this link in the show notes and folks can click on each of these and there's a lot more explanation of what it is you're thinking about there. Awesome. Okay, just a couple more questions.
turns.zh: 惊人的。最后一张。小型微调模型作为巨大通用模型的替代品。是的。甜的。因此，我们将在节目注释中包含此链接，人们可以单击其中的每一个，并且有更多关于您正在考虑的内容的解释。惊人的。好的，还有几个问题。

turns.speaker: Dalton Caldwell
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: One is just your background. So from what I've read, in the early 2000s, you were basically hanging out with some of the biggest success stories of today. Folks like Zuck and Reid Hoffman, Sam Altman, Elon, Sean Parker. This is before they really became anyone and they all became very successful. I'm curious just looking back at that, what you've noticed is consistent across these folks that ended up being really successful over time.
turns.zh: 一是你的背景。据我所知，在 2000 年代初，人们基本上都在关注当今一些最伟大的成功故事。像扎克和里德·霍夫曼、萨姆·奥尔特曼、埃隆、肖恩·帕克这样的人。这是在他们真正成为任何人并且都变得非常成功之前。我很好奇，回顾一下，你注意到这些人的情况是一致的，随着时间的推移，他们最终取得了真正的成功。

turns.speaker: Dalton Caldwell
turns.en: Back in 2003, being in Silicon Valley and being interested in startups, it was a really small space. There just weren't that many people that were into this stuff. And so I remember I cold emailed Reid Hoffman when LinkedIn was 12 employees and he just responded and he's like, "Oh, let's have lunch." He was just a guy and everyone else that was doing, I guess you could call it social networking, that was the people that I knew. There was a few conferences you would go to and there'd be 30 people there. It reminds me of stories about the Homebrew Computer Club. I'm not saying this is as cool. But when I read stories about what it was like when the Homebrew Computer Club existed, it was a very small number of people that all knew each other that were real weirdo outsiders that were into this stuff, okay? And so that's what in the post.com boom Bay Area startup scene, that's legitimately what it felt like. (00:57:03): And so I didn't think a lot about the personality traits of these people. Again, they were all pretty different people, but what they had in common is the folks that are now the really big names just had a lot of staying power. Right? So when I met Sam, he had dropped out of Stanford to work on Loot, which is hilariously a way to find people around you to hang out with. An interesting theme here, huh? He was cool. He was this really young guy and he just did that. It wasn't huge. And then he got into other stuff and ended up working at YC, ended up getting involved in hard tech and has now reinvented himself as the big mind behind AI, which again, awesome. But if I think about who he was back in the day, yeah, he was a 23-year-old working on a thing for feature phones to find friends in your neighborhood. (00:57:58): Their customer was Boost Mobile. I bet you could go find the commercials for Loot that Boost Mobile put out on YouTube. Those are actually pretty funny. Have you seen those commercials?
turns.zh: 早在 2003 年，当时在硅谷，对初创公司很感兴趣，那里的空间非常小。只是没有那么多人喜欢这个东西。所以我记得当 LinkedIn 仅有 12 名员工时，我给 Reid Hoffman 发了一封冷冷的电子邮件，他只是回复了，“哦，我们吃午饭吧。”他只是一个人，其他人都在做，我想你可以称之为社交网络，那是我认识的人。你会去参加一些会议，那里有 30 个人。这让我想起了自制计算机俱乐部的故事。我并不是说这很酷。但是，当我读到有关自制计算机俱乐部存在时的情况时，只有极少数互相认识的人是真正对这些东西感兴趣的奇怪的局外人，好吗？这就是后网络繁荣时期湾区创业场景中的情况，这就是合理的感觉。 (00:57:03)：所以我并没有过多考虑这些人的性格特征。再说一遍，他们都是截然不同的人，但他们的共同点是，现在真正的大牌人物都有很强的持久力。正确的？所以当我遇到 Sam 时，他已经从斯坦福大学退学，去 Loot 工作，这是一种有趣的方式来找到你周围的人一起出去玩。这里有一个有趣的主题，是吧？他很酷。他是一个非常年轻的小伙子，他就是这么做的。它并不大。然后他开始涉足其他领域，最终在 YC 工作，最终涉足硬技术，现在将自己重塑为人工智能背后的大智者，这再次非常棒。但如果我想想他当时是谁，是的，他是一个 23 岁的年轻人，致力于通过功能手机寻找附近的朋友。 (00:57:58)：他们的客户是 Boost Mobile。我打赌你可以找到 Boost Mobile 在 YouTube 上发布的 Loot 广告。这些实际上很有趣。你看过那些广告吗？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: No, but I'm going to go check them out.
turns.zh: 不，但我要去看看他们。

turns.speaker: Dalton Caldwell
turns.en: Anyway, it's pretty funny. So yeah, that's the real story. And then, yeah, I remember I was in downtown Palo Alto at the time, and some of the folks I was friends with were friends with Sean Parker, and this was actually before Sean Parker went to Facebook. He was part of Napster. And so one of my friends was like, "Oh, we need to get my friend a ride to the airport." And so I ended up giving Sean Parker a ride to the Oakland Airport. And again, what was he like? I don't know. He just basically sat in the back seat on the phone the whole time. But again, my point is I wasn't like, "Wow, these are going to be really big successful people that one day will be important in the world." It just felt like a bunch of nerds that really liked the internet and computers, doing things that they were interested in and were just obsessed with this. (00:58:57): They weren't like, "Gee, should I move to New York?" Or, "Maybe I should go to law school." It was people that were very bought in to staying working on internet companies. And so you'll see these folks just reinvent themselves multiple eras, right? Okay, like Reid Hoffman, he worked at PayPal, right? And then he did LinkedIn and then he was a VC. He's had all these different eras where it's the same person, but it's almost like a different figure, right?
turns.zh: 不管怎样，这很有趣。是的，这就是真实的故事。然后，是的，我记得当时我在帕洛阿尔托市中心，我的一些朋友也是肖恩·帕克的朋友，而这实际上是在肖恩·帕克加入 Facebook 之前。他是 Napster 的成员。我的一个朋友说：“哦，我们需要搭车去机场。”所以我最终载了肖恩·帕克去奥克兰机场。再说一次，他是什么样的人？我不知道。他基本上一直坐在后座打电话。但我再说一次，我的观点是，我并不是想，“哇，这些人将成为非常成功的人，有一天会在世界上变得很重要。”感觉就像一群真正喜欢互联网和计算机的书呆子，做他们感兴趣的事情，并且对此着迷。 (00:58:57)：他们不会说，“哎呀，我应该搬到纽约吗？”或者，“也许我应该去法学院。”人们非常愿意留在互联网公司工作。所以你会看到这些人在多个时代重塑自己，对吗？好吧，就像 Reid Hoffman 一样，他也在 PayPal 工作，对吗？然后他做了LinkedIn，然后他成为了一名风险投资家。他经历过很多不同的时代，虽然是同一个人，但几乎就像是不同的人物，对吧？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: There's a lot of interesting lessons there. One is that your career is long and you'll have the opportunity to do many things and you can continue to shift. In my example, this is my fourth career, I realized. I was an engineer, then a founder, then a product manager, now whatever this job is. And I think that's really common. I think the other, again, is the personality types point, which I didn't comment on, but I think it's so important that you can be super introverted and be super successful. You can be super extroverted and be very successful. And I think the key there is use your skills and strengths to achieve the same things. You don't have to be the amazing presenter on Steve Jobs type stage. You can do the same thing in a different way. And then the other point there is, again, coming back to you just need to be really excited and enjoy the work you're doing because that'll drive you forward and make you be successful. So I like that the story is a summary of so many of the things you've shared so far. (01:00:21): There's other two other fun stories, maybe pick one. The other one is you sold your startup to MySpace and your job was basically to save MySpace. And then the other is you're the reason Andreessen Horowitz missed out on Instagram and couldn't invest. So which of those would you want to share?
turns.zh: 那里有很多有趣的课程。一是你的职业生涯很长，你会有机会做很多事情，你可以不断地转变。在我的例子中，我意识到这是我的第四份职业。我是一名工程师，然后是创始人，然后是产品经理，现在无论这份工作是什么。我认为这很常见。我认为另一个是性格类型点，我没有对此发表评论，但我认为这非常重要，因为你可以超级内向并取得超级成功。你可以非常外向并且非常成功。我认为关键是利用你的技能和优势来实现同样的目标。您不必成为史蒂夫·乔布斯式舞台上出色的演讲者。你可以用不同的方式做同样的事情。另一点是，再次回到你身上，你只需要感到非常兴奋并享受你正在做的工作，因为这会推动你前进并让你取得成功。所以我喜欢这个故事是对你迄今为止分享的许多事情的总结。 (01:00:21)：还有另外两个有趣的故事，也许选一个。另一种情况是，您将自己的初创公司卖给了 MySpace，而您的工作基本上就是拯救 MySpace。另一个是你是 Andreessen Horowitz 错过 Instagram 且无法投资的原因。那么您想分享其中哪一个？

turns.speaker: Dalton Caldwell
turns.en: Well, it's the same story. And the way that it's the same story is my second company... Basically, I sold my first company to MySpace. It was the music company that I worked on. And they recruited a new CEO who was formerly the COO of Facebook called Owen Van Natta. So again, hilariously part of the same little circle of people. And Owen was like, "Okay, we need to fix MySpace. Rupert Murdoch's got the juice. He wants me to fix it. We're going to do it. So come up with some ideas." And the best idea that I could come up with at the time was doing something around mobile photo sharing, something like Twitter, but for photos. And I figured with MySpace's user base, that would work pretty well. This was in 2010, so it was right as the App Store was getting big, and I had a lot of success in the App Store with imeem. It was one of the top downloaded music apps. And so I was like, "Wow, the App Store was really good." And I was really into apps being the thing. (01:01:40): And at this time, Facebook was a little early on. They were trying to do cross-platform mobile apps, if you recall. And their apps were not great. This was, again, ancient history. So that was my plan. And then immediately Owen Van Natta was fired, and so I didn't even really get onboarded. And so I just left. I think I worked in MySpace for a month because the person that acquired my company got fired and I think the whole word chart got fired. I didn't even know who to talk to. It was really great. It was a great experience. You know what I'm saying? I wasn't really sure who my point of contact was at that point. I don't think they knew either. It was just a mess.
turns.zh: 嗯，这是同一个故事。我的第二家公司也是如此……基本上，我将我的第一家公司卖给了 MySpace。这是我工作的音乐公司。他们还聘请了一位新的首席执行官，他是 Facebook 的前首席运营官，名叫欧文·范纳塔 (Owen Van Natta)。再次，滑稽地属于同一个小圈子。欧文说：“好吧，我们需要修复 MySpace。鲁珀特·默多克有能力。他希望我修复它。我们会这么做的。所以想出一些想法。”我当时能想到的最好的主意就是围绕移动照片共享做一些事情，比如 Twitter，但针对的是照片。我认为根据 MySpace 的用户群，这会很有效。那是在 2010 年，随着 App Store 的规模不断壮大，我的 imeem 在 App Store 上取得了很大的成功。它是下载次数最多的音乐应用程序之一。所以我就想，“哇，App Store 真的很棒。”我真的很喜欢应用程序。 (01:01:40)：此时 Facebook 的发展有点早。如果您还记得的话，他们正在尝试开发跨平台移动应用程序。他们的应用程序也不是很好。这又是古老的历史了。这就是我的计划。然后欧文·范纳塔立即被解雇了，所以我什至没有真正加入。于是我就离开了。我想我在 MySpace 工作了一个月，因为收购我公司的人被解雇了，而且我认为整个单词图表都被解雇了。我什至不知道该和谁说话。真的很棒。这是一次很棒的经历。你知道我在说什么吗？那时我不太确定我的联系人是谁。我想他们也不知道。简直是一团糟。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Just message Tom.
turns.zh: 只需给汤姆发消息即可。

turns.speaker: Dalton Caldwell
turns.en: No, no. He was long gone. Seriously. I know you're kidding. But no, literally, I don't know who was left at that point. Tom was long gone. And so I was like, "Well, I should just do a new startup and I should work on something like what I was thinking about." And I ended up starting the company and quickly was able to raise an angel around because people remembered my company from the first one. And the major investor we had was Andreessen Horowitz. This is one of their first board seat investments, like Marc Andreessen was on my board. And again, I have my own set of stories about that, but it was interesting experience and we launched it in... I think we got half a million or a million users. You can go find tech print articles about it. We launched on Android and iOS and it was mobile photo sharing, and actually it was growing pretty well. Okay? (01:03:11): And then what happened is there was another portfolio company called Bourbon, which was originally a ForceWare clone that was built by these two guys. And they decided to pivot out of that and into what... Which was pretty similar to my thing. Again, fair enough, that's just how this works. And they did something smart. Again, this is just me talking, I don't know what their version of the story is. But what I think they did that was smart is if you looked on the paid app store charts, the number one app was Hipstamatic and Hipstamatic cost money. And what do we know about what people want? They want things that are free that cost money, right? And so they basically built a pretty legitimate knockoff of the Hipstamatic filters, combining it with a social graph, and they launched it and it pretty quickly took off. So of course this is Instagram, right? And so it took off really quickly and that was a wild experience for me to be like, "Oh, this seems familiar." (01:04:07): And basically because Andreessen Horowitz had invested in my company, was on the board, even though they were investors in Instagram, that was a conflict and they didn't do the deal. And then for whatever reason, this became a big source of Silicon Valley gossip, which was like, "Wow, I can't believe this happened." And so it was just a really weird experience for me as a founder to be right in the middle of something that became culturally so important.
turns.zh: 不，不。他已经走了很久了。严重地。我知道你在开玩笑。但不，从字面上看，我不知道当时留下了谁。汤姆早已不在了。所以我想，“好吧，我应该做一个新的创业公司，我应该做一些像我在想的事情。”我最终创办了这家公司，并很快就培养了一位天使投资人，因为人们从第一家公司就记住了我的公司。我们的主要投资者是 Andreessen Horowitz。这是他们的第一个董事会席位投资之一，就像马克·安德森 (Marc Andreessen) 是我的董事会成员一样。再说一次，我有自己的一套关于这方面的故事，但这是一次有趣的经历，我们推出它的......我认为我们有五十万或一百万用户。您可以去查找有关它的技术印刷文章。我们在 Android 和 iOS 上推出了移动照片共享功能，实际上它发展得相当不错。好的？ (01:03:11)：然后发生的事情是，还有一家名为 Bourbon 的投资组合公司，它最初是由这两个人创建的 ForceWare 克隆版。他们决定摆脱这个，转向……这与我的事情非常相似。再说一次，公平地说，这就是它的工作原理。他们做了一些聪明的事情。再说一次，这只是我在说，我不知道他们的故事版本是什么。但我认为他们的做法很聪明，如果你查看付费应用商店排行榜，排名第一的应用程序是 Hipstamatic，而 Hipstamatic 是要花钱的。我们对人们的需求了解多少？他们想要的是免费但需要花钱的东西，对吗？因此，他们基本上构建了一个相当合法的 Hipstamatic 过滤器仿制品，将其与社交图谱相结合，然后他们推出了它，并且很快就取得了成功。这当然是Instagram，对吧？所以它很快就起飞了，这对我来说是一次疯狂的经历，“哦，这看起来很熟悉。” (01:04:07)：基本上是因为 Andreessen Horowitz 投资了我的公司，并且是董事会成员，尽管他们是 Instagram 的投资者，但这是一个冲突，他们没有做这笔交易。然后，无论出于何种原因，这成为硅谷八卦的一个重要来源，就像“哇，我不敢相信这发生了。”因此，作为一名创始人，我正处于一个在文化上变得如此重要的事情之中，这真是一次非常奇怪的经历。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I imagine there's a bullseye in your back from a16z for a little bit.
turns.zh: 我想你的背上有一点来自 a16z 的靶心。

turns.speaker: Dalton Caldwell
turns.en: Oh, I don't actually think they care. I don't think they held it against me because what did I do wrong?
turns.zh: 哦，我实际上并不认为他们关心。我不认为他们因为我做错了什么而反对我？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's true.
turns.zh: 这是真的。

turns.speaker: Dalton Caldwell
turns.en: I started a company. You know what I'm saying? Obviously there was some frustration, but I was guy who had a company that they invested in. I don't know. I didn't feel didn't much higher for them. I think this is just how life works.
turns.zh: 我创办了一家公司。你知道我在说什么吗？显然有一些挫败感，但我是拥有一家他们投资的公司的人。我不知道。我不觉得他们的水平高多少。我认为这就是生活的方式。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. I wonder if they changed their conflict policies after that at all.
turns.zh: 是的。我想知道他们在那之后是否改变了他们的冲突政策。

turns.speaker: Dalton Caldwell
turns.en: I don't think so. I think this has happened multiple other times, but those aren't my stories to tell.
turns.zh: 我不这么认为。我认为这种情况已经发生过多次，但这些不是我要讲的故事。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And by the way, I don't know if you mentioned the name of your startup, it was called PicPlz, right?
turns.zh: 顺便说一句，我不知道你是否提到过你的初创公司的名字，它的名字叫PicPlz，对吧？

turns.speaker: Dalton Caldwell
turns.en: Yeah, it's called PicPlz. Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的，它的名字叫PicPlz。是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Great. Okay. So for the final phase before we get to very exciting lighting round, I have these two segments, recurring segments. I have failure corner and contrarian corner. We can do both or we can pick one or the other. Failure corner, share a story of a time in your career where you failed and when you learned from that experience. Contrarian corner, what's something you believe that most other people don't believe?
turns.zh: 伟大的。好的。因此，在我们进入非常令人兴奋的灯光回合之前的最后阶段，我有这两个部分，重复的部分。我有失败角和逆向角。我们可以两者都做，也可以选择其中之一。失败角，分享您职业生涯中失败的经历以及您从失败中吸取教训的故事。逆向角落，有什么是你相信但大多数人不相信的事情？

turns.speaker: Dalton Caldwell
turns.en: Yeah, I think for contrarian corner, I know where I would start and I think it's relevant for your listener. I think this is relevant to this and you could argue this isn't contrary, but here's what I think. I think growth and growth hacking and doing all this analytics, A/B testing stuff, is a total waste of time for very early startups. And that one of the weird things about having lots of startup advice on the internet, again, this is one of the reasons we started making videos at YC, is a lot of the advice was catered towards later stage companies. Like, "Oh, here's how you set up your board and here's how you motivate your sales team." It was all aimed at series A, series B founders, and not for seed stage founders. The problem was seed stage founders would consume all the later stage advice and get really confused. (01:06:35): And so the anti-pattern I see is there are lots of founders that are very familiar with your awesome work, which again, I really recommend, I like it. But when you have no customers and you're reading Lenny's guides on how to set up split testing and how you did growth at Airbnb, oh man, that is so dumb. That is so not helpful. And so you see this inclination away from getting a first customer, getting one customer and talking to that person, and instead they have all this really complex growth hacking theory. I think this also happens if you worked in big tech where your product already has scale. And so if you work at Facebook and your job is to launch new little features, yeah, of course you should make heavy use of analytics and A/B testing and split testing and feature flags. Yeah, yeah, yeah, makes sense. But when you have no users, what are you doing? So do you think that's contrary? What do you think? I'm just trying to argue this advice applied to a startup that's too early is actively not helpful.
turns.zh: 是的，我认为对于逆向角落，我知道我会从哪里开始，我认为这与你的听众相关。我认为这与此相关，你可能会说这并不矛盾，但这就是我的想法。我认为增长和增长黑客以及所有这些分析、A/B 测试的东西，对于非常早期的初创公司来说完全是浪费时间。互联网上有大量创业建议的奇怪之处之一是，很多建议都是针对后期公司的，这也是我们开始在 YC 制作视频的原因之一。就像，“哦，这就是你如何建立你的董事会，这就是你如何激励你的销售团队。”它都是针对 A 轮、B 轮创始人，而不是种子阶段创始人。问题是种子阶段的创始人会吸收所有后期阶段的建议并感到非常困惑。 (01:06:35)：所以我看到的反模式是有很多创始人非常熟悉你出色的工作，我再次强烈推荐，我喜欢它。但是，当你没有客户，而你正在阅读 Lenny 的关于如何设置对比测试以及如何在 Airbnb 实现增长的指南时，天哪，这太愚蠢了。那是没有帮助的。因此，你会发现这种倾向远离了获得第一个客户，获得一个客户并与该人交谈，相反，他们拥有所有这些非常复杂的增长黑客理论。我认为如果你在大型科技公司工作并且你的产品已经具有规模，这种情况也会发生。所以，如果你在 Facebook 工作，你的工作是推出新的小功能，是的，你当然应该大量使用分析、A/B 测试、对比测试和功能标志。是啊是啊，有道理。但是当你没有用户时，你在做什么？那么你认为这是相反的吗？你怎么认为？我只是想论证这个建议应用于太早的初创公司实际上没有帮助。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I think it's contrarian for many people. 100%. I also 100% agree with it. It makes me feel like I need to, at the top of my post, share here's who this is for. If you're earlier than this, ignore it. If you're later than this, ignore it.
turns.zh: 我认为这对很多人来说都是逆向思维。 100%。我也百分百同意。这让我觉得我需要在帖子的顶部分享这是给谁的。如果你比这更早，请忽略它。如果你晚于此，请忽略它。

turns.speaker: Dalton Caldwell
turns.en: I mean, again, I'm not saying you do anything wrong, but imagine if the OG Airbnb founders took all of your current advice and applied it when they had four users and they knew their names and they were trying to run complicated growth hacking split testings.
turns.zh: 我的意思是，我并不是说你做错了什么，但想象一下，如果 OG Airbnb 创始人采纳了你当前的所有建议，并在他们有四个用户并且知道他们的名字并且试图运行复杂的增长黑客对比测试时应用它。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. Maybe just to clarify when you talk about growth hacking. So obviously when you're starting something, say a consumer app, you need to get a bunch of users somehow. What's your sense of just when you say don't do this sort of thing, but this is okay? What falls in those buckets?
turns.zh: 是的。也许只是为了在谈论增长黑客时澄清一下。很明显，当你开始做某件事时，比如消费者应用程序，你需要以某种方式获得一批用户。当你说不要做这种事但没关系时，你的感觉是什么？这些桶里会掉什么？

turns.speaker: Dalton Caldwell
turns.en: I think it depends on the idea. I think in the case of Whatnot, it was consumer app and they needed to get users. But they were very intellectually honest on the metrics for how you get a marketplace off the ground. And they didn't just go dump all their money into Instagram ads. They effectively knew they needed to focus on buyers and on the buy side and build momentum on the buy side. They really understood marketplaces. And so for consumer, I think it's having a sophisticated view of how you get the consumer company off the ground. I think if you look at the Facebook story, them getting a hundred percent penetration on the Harvard campus first instead of launching overall. Again, good strategy, would recommend that strategy. So again, the way to extrapolate that is know what your comps are of what companies you... Or type is, and then look at what they did on the zero to one and ignore what they do today. Right? (01:09:20): Don't pay attention to what Facebook does today if you're a brand new startup founder, pay attention to Facebook when they were getting their first thousand users. What were those tactics?
turns.zh: 我认为这取决于想法。我认为就 Whatnot 而言，它是消费者应用程序，他们需要吸引用户。但他们对于如何启动市场的指标非常诚实。他们并没有把所有的钱都投入到 Instagram 广告中。他们实际上知道他们需要关注买家和买方，并为买方建立动力。他们真正了解市场。因此，对于消费者来说，我认为它对如何让消费者公司起步有一个复杂的看法。我想如果你看看 Facebook 的故事，你会发现他们首先在哈佛校园获得了 100% 的渗透率，而不是全面推出。再说一遍，好的策略，会推荐该策略。再说一次，推断的方法是知道你的公司的比较是什么......或输入的是，然后看看他们在零到一上做了什么，忽略他们今天做了什么。正确的？ (01:09:20)：如果你是一个全新的初创公司创始人，请不要关注 Facebook 今天在做什么，而应该关注 Facebook 刚刚获得第一批 1000 个用户时的情况。这些战术是什么？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I feel like this should be its own episode where we just go into how to get your first thousand users. I know there's a video actually we'll link to that Gustav made with YC's advice on how to get your users. Did you want to visit failure corner or not? Or shall we move on?
turns.zh: 我觉得这应该是它自己的一集，我们只讨论如何获得第一批一千名用户。我知道实际上我们会链接到 Gustav 制作的一个视频，其中包含 YC 关于如何吸引用户的建议。你想不想参观失败角落？或者我们继续前进？

turns.speaker: Dalton Caldwell
turns.en: I failed at tons of stuff. As an investor, I make lots of bad investments as well as good ones. I think in my startups I pivoted a lot and a lot of things I did didn't work out. And so again, I just gave you a specific story with PicPlz, right? You just heard a specific story there. I guess what I learned is that you just can't let it get to you too much and you got to keep going. And that if you keep going, no one really remembers those as much and it doesn't really define you. Fear of failure shouldn't dominate all of your thoughts. And instead you should use your energy and positivity to keep trying to do good work, right? Because back in the day, if I would've been like, "Well, I guess startups aren't for me, I guess tech isn't for me." I wouldn't have had a career doing any of this stuff. I wouldn't be working at YC, I wouldn't be advising companies, right? (01:10:36): So I always had to have in my life a lot of optimism and energy and use that energy and motor to keep me going. And it served me really well, right? Even if lots of stuff I tried didn't work and continue to not work. Again, obvious stuff I know, but yeah, that doesn't mean it's not true, even though it's obvious.

turns.speaker: Dalton Caldwell
turns.en: Yeah, I guess the final thought is if someone wants to do a startup and doesn't know where to start, just to give you permission to talk to potential customers and try to pre-sell something before you write code and have those conversations.
